title: McNulty Shocks the Cycling World with 'Miracle' World Championship Win
summary:
Brandon McNulty wasn't supposed to win. He wasn't even among the pre-race favourites — not like former world champion Remco Evenepoel or young stars Isaac del Toro and Paul Seixas. But on Sunday in Montreal, the 28-year-old American pulled off what he called "a miracle" to capture the men's elite road race at the UCI Road World Championships.

McNulty attacked with 33 kilometres remaining and never gave up the lead. He finished the 273.4-kilometre course in 6 hours, 17 minutes and 4 seconds — just 13 seconds ahead of Australia's Michael Matthews, who took silver in 6:17:17. Matthew van der Poel of the Netherlands earned bronze.

The course included 12 laps of a 13.4-kilometre circuit packed with enthusiastic fans, and the race was chaotic and unpredictable, partly because two-time defending champion Tadej Pogacar was absent, recovering from a crash. Without the Slovenian star, the field was wide open.

"Until the last 300 metres, I really didn't even believe it," McNulty said. "I was just dying, but I just kept pushing." He added: "I'm at a loss for words."

His lead shrank to just 10 seconds with 10 kilometres to go, but none of the chasers could close the gap. Van der Poel launched an attack with 6.8 kilometres left, but it fizzled out.

McNulty became the first American to win this title since Lance Armstrong in 1993. Armstrong congratulated him afterward.

"We've said for weeks that we have a super strong team and that it's possible. We rode crazy well. We marked everything, had guys ahead," McNulty said. "I knew something could happen but it would take a miracle. I guess today, a miracle happened."

Canadian riders had a tough day. Michael Leonard of Oakville, Ont., was the top Canadian in 32nd place in 6:23:43. Michael Woods of Toronto finished 35th in 6:23:52 in his final race, while Nickolas Zukowsky of Sainte-Lucie-des-Laurentides, Que., was 45th. Several Canadians, including Hugo Houle on his birthday, did not finish.
why_it_matters: It shows how quickly a sport can flip when its dominant figure is missing — and why single-day championships are the most unpredictable races in cycling. It also matters for cycling's growth in North America, where a home-grown world champion can bring in new fans and sponsors.

background_read: The UCI Road World Championships (run by the UCI, cycling's global governing body) is a one-day race, not a three-week tour. The winner wears the rainbow jersey for a whole year, and riders race for their national teams rather than their normal professional teams.

Remco Evenepoel (the Belgian who won the world title in 2022) and Tadej Pogacar (the Slovenian who has won the Tour de France several times and took the world title in 2024) were the big names everyone expected to fight for the win. When Pogacar pulled out through injury, outsiders suddenly had a real chance.

Montreal, the largest city in the Canadian province of Quebec, hosted the race on a short city circuit that the riders lapped twelve times — a format that gives the crowd a big role, because fans see the race pass again and again.

Lance Armstrong (the American who won this title in 1993 and later had his seven Tour de France victories stripped for doping) shows how long the United States had waited for another road race world champion.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the underdog and his team
perspectives.description: McNulty and his national team proved that preparation and teamwork can beat reputation. He attacked at exactly the right moment and his teammates marked every dangerous move, so a rider nobody picked ended up in the rainbow jersey.

Some fans will say the race carried an asterisk because the two-time defending champion Pogacar never started. A world title won without the sport's biggest name in the field is still a title, but it leaves an argument that will never be settled.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the nature of one-day racing
perspectives.description: Historically, single-day world championships are far more random than three-week tours, because one bad moment or one well-timed attack decides everything. That unpredictability is exactly why the sport values the rainbow jersey so highly.

Winning the world title reshapes McNulty's career: more pressure, more attention and a different role on his team. It also raises the question of whether the United States can build a deeper group of riders around him.
